paper_metadata.title: Novel Co-free high performance TRIP and TWIP medium-entropy alloys at cryogenic temperatures

evidence.quote: In this work, novel Co-free FexMn75-xNi10Cr15 (x=50 and 55 at.%) MEAs were developed, which exhibit a good combination of low cost, high strength and ductility at cryogenic temperature.

Apparently, all the MEAs clearly revealed a single FCC phase structure within the limit of XRD instrument resolution.
Only FCC phase exists in both Fe50 and Fe55 MEAs, which is consistent with the XRD results in Fig. 1.

It can be seen from the IPF maps that the equiaxed grain structures were observed in both the Fe50 and Fe55 MEA samples before tensile deformation (Fig. 2 (a1) and (b1)). The average grain size was estimated to be ~15 μm for Fe50 MEA
The average grain size was estimated to be ~15 μm for Fe50 MEA and ~10 μm for Fe55 MEA.
Abundant twin boundaries exist in both Fe50 and Fe55 MEAs, as shown in red lines (Fig. 2(a2) and (b2)), indicating that both Fe50 and Fe55 MEAs might have a relative low stacking fault energy (SFE).
Abundant twin boundaries exist in both Fe50 and Fe55 MEAs, as shown in red lines (Fig. 2(a2) and (b2)).

The higher fraction of HCP phase and higher degree of grain elongation were observed in the fractured sample at 77 K than that at 293 K, indicating the strain-induced FCC-to-HCP phase transformation occurs at 77 K.

The EBSD IPF maps and phase maps of Fe55 MEA after fracture at 77 K in Fig. 6 reveal that more FCC phase (~26%) are transformed into HCP phase after fracture at 77 K, but appears less twin boundaries.

These “TRIP effect” during cryogenic-temperature deformation are responsible for the ultra-high SHR of Fe50 MEA (Fig. 3(b)), which delays the onset of necking, resulting in excellent combination of cryogenic strength and ductility.

In addition, the abundant mechanical twinning in the Fe50 MEA also leads to a dynamic Hall-Petch effect (Fig. 5(b2)). The TWIP effect is also advantageous for the Fe50 MEA to have a higher ductility at 77 K
the formation of HCP plates reduces the mean free path of dislocations [16, 30], which is similar to the dynamic Hall–Patch effect.
